lesson.title: Why the Reward Can Backfire: Intrinsic vs Extrinsic Motivation
lesson.summary: Intrinsic motivation means doing something because it is inherently interesting or satisfying, extrinsic motivation means doing something to earn a reward or avoid a punishment, and research on the overjustification effect shows the two can interact in surprising, sometimes counterproductive, ways.
lesson.body:
Self-determination theory frames intrinsic motivation as the clearest expression of autonomy, competence, and relatedness all being satisfied at once: a person engages in an activity simply because they want to, with no external push required. Extrinsic motivation, by contrast, involves doing something because of a separate outcome the activity leads to, a reward, a grade, a paycheck, or the avoidance of some punishment or disapproval. Deci and Ryan's broader model treats extrinsic motivation as itself a spectrum, ranging from motivation that feels entirely externally controlled to motivation that has been more fully internalized and accepted as one's own, but the basic intrinsic versus extrinsic distinction remains one of the most useful and well supported ideas in the study of motivation.

A particularly important and well replicated finding is the overjustification effect: adding a salient extrinsic reward to an activity a person already finds intrinsically enjoyable can, under certain conditions, reduce their later interest in that activity once the reward is no longer available. The classic demonstration comes from a study by Lepper, Greene, and Nisbett in the early 1970s, in which preschool children who already enjoyed drawing on their own were divided into groups. Children who were told in advance they would receive a reward for drawing, and then received it, later spent less free time drawing on their own compared to children who received no reward or who received the same reward unexpectedly, with no prior promise attached to it.

The proposed explanation fits neatly with self-determination theory's emphasis on autonomy. When a reward is made salient and expected in advance, a person may unconsciously reinterpret their own motivation, shifting from an internal explanation, I do this because I enjoy it, to an external one, I do this to get the reward. That shift can undercut the sense that the behavior is self-chosen, which is precisely the ingredient self-determination theory identifies as central to intrinsic motivation.

It is worth being careful not to overgeneralize this finding. The undermining effect appears most reliably when the reward is expected in advance and prominently tied to simply doing the activity, rather than being unexpected or tied to genuine achievement, and it applies most clearly to activities a person already found intrinsically enjoyable to begin with. Rewards for activities people were never particularly intrinsically motivated to do, routine chores or rote practice, generally do not show this same backfire effect, and can be a perfectly reasonable and effective tool. The practical lesson is not that rewards are always harmful, it is that turning an already loved activity into something done chiefly for an external prize carries a real, demonstrated risk of quietly eroding the love that was there in the first place.
